positive.original:
This is the best game I have ever played in my entire life. After I watched LOTS of lore videos, I started to appreciate this game even more. The lore is so deep in this trilogy it is INSANE. Every game is connected to eachother in so many ways. It is mindblowing. When you will play it, you will understand what I mean.

Enough of the lore let's talk about the best part in this game bosses. Peak Souls 3 has the best bosses of any video game. Most of my favorite bosses I have encountered in my life are from this game as well as the best one (Slave Knight Gale). I will not spoil the fun for you. Just know It is PEAK. I will admit there are a ton of gimic bosses however, there also incredible and unique ones. The music, design, attacks, animations, etc.--everything about these bosses is just amazing. The music from the final boss haunts me to this day because of how incredible it is. Music in this game is phenomenal and for sure some of the pieces will be remembered for a long time.

Many people hate this game for how linear it is and I don't really understand why. In my opinion it is better than a kind of open world in ds1. In ds3 you cannot really get lost. If you do that is a skill issue. Even though it is a straight line it still works perfectly and the exploration feels great and rewarding. Also the level design is incredible. Of course, there are some bad areas but they are more than made up for the beatiful ones such as Irithyll of The Boreal Valley. Everytime I play through this game I melt when I see that view.

A friend recommended this game to me when I was pretty new to pc gaming. I cannot express how grateful I am for that. This game alone changed how I look at games now and how I play them. Because of this game alone I played every other Fromsoftware title. I cannot express and no one can how incredible this game is. 

This is a must play for any gamer. 100000/10 

(P.S. I want to recommend a guy on yt that played through dark souls games blind and how amazed he was by all of them. His channel is Bind)

positive.original:
[h1]Peak Souls 3 — Suffering perfected[/h1]

After getting the platinum in [url=https://store.steampowered.com/agecheck/app/1245620/][b]Elden Ring[/b][/url], I wanted to dive deeper into the Souls-like genre, and my next stop was Dark Souls III. I went in seeing it through the lens of Elden Ring, which was my first real experience with this kind of game.

Right away, you can feel the difference. Unlike the open world of Elden Ring, Dark Souls III is much more linear and focused. For me, that actually worked in its favor — the minimal branching lets you concentrate on what really matters: the fights, not wandering around looking for random loot. And it doesn’t make the game feel shorter, it just keeps you from getting distracted by pointless activities.

Another thing I loved is that the game gives you all the tools you need right from the start. You don’t have to grind or level up artificially — just move forward and clear areas, and it happens so naturally that you barely notice your character leveling up.

The world and atmosphere, in my opinion, are even stronger than in Elden Ring. Dark, dying environments, the music, and level design all work together to create a really immersive, oppressive feeling. The soundtrack is top-notch and perfectly matches the action.

I also really liked how your role in the world feels. In Elden Ring, you’re constantly treated like some chosen one, the only worthy hero, yet even normal enemies can still one-shot you late in the game. In Dark Souls III, it feels much more logical — you’re not some special savior, just one of many undead doing your part, a tiny cog in a huge machine. And that fits the world perfectly.

Boss fights were much more enjoyable too. They feel fairer: no long attack delays where the boss just swings and then pauses forever, and no constant AoE attacks that, in Elden Ring, aren’t about difficulty but about taking away your ability to dodge — they just break your rolls and make it more likely you’ll get hit. Here it’s all about reaction, timing, and understanding the fight.

The only boss that let me down was the Nameless King. The first phase mostly felt like fighting the camera rather than the boss, and the second phase is just poking at a big, slow enemy with a limited set of attacks. It’s not hard, it’s just tedious and kinda dull.

Overall, Dark Souls III turned out to be a perfect follow-up after Elden Ring. More linear, more focused, and in many ways fairer — the experience feels tight and memorable. I also got the platinum, which mostly just stands out because of the long covenant grind, but even years after release, there are still plenty of enthusiasts around to lend a hand.

9/10

In Dark Souls III, it feels much more logical — you’re not some special savior, just one of many undead doing your part, a tiny cog in a huge machine. And that fits the world perfectly.

Boss fights were much more enjoyable too. They feel fairer: no long attack delays where the boss just swings and then pauses forever, and no constant AoE attacks that, in Elden Ring, aren’t about difficulty but about taking away your ability to dodge — they just break your rolls and make it more likely you’ll get hit. Here it’s all about reaction, timing, and understanding the fight.

The only boss that let me down was the Nameless King. The first phase mostly felt like fighting the camera rather than the boss, and the second phase is just poking at a big, slow enemy with a limited set of attacks. It’s not hard, it’s just tedious and kinda dull.

Overall, Dark Souls III turned out to be a perfect follow-up after Elden Ring. More linear, more focused, and in many ways fairer — the experience feels tight and memorable. I also got the platinum, which mostly just stands out because of the long covenant grind, but even years after release, there are still plenty of enthusiasts around to lend a hand.

9/10

positive.original:
[i] PC + PS4 playtime is probably close to 400 hours. [/i]

I love Dark Souls III. It’s the one I come back to the most because it’s simply the most fun to play gameplay wise in the trilogy, and maybe even in the entire Souls series.

That said, I still prefer Dark Souls I for its atmosphere.

Dark Souls III has the best bosses, the best gameplay, and the most consistent design across the trilogy. But it also feels like the moment FromSoftware leaned more into a faster, anime-like fighting style, which I’m not particularly a fan of.

Even so, it remains an incredibly fun game and one I revisit more than any other Souls title.

positive.original:
GORGEOUS... The Level and Game Design is insane and that is an understatement, the graphics are for a 2016 game (bought in 2026) timeless aaand... GORGEOUS...

If you are not scared of some deathscreens and love a little challenge (which can be cheesed many times because of amazing Game Design and your own choices how tho handle tricky situations - and i love cheese in this game and in real life, no i am not addicted, i have no problems, everything is fine)

You are playing a little character in this large world and have to estimate situations all the time to become the strongest, there are many challenges waiting for you and a lot of decisions to make and dont mind getting your bussines getting mixed up with these pesky invaders, dont forget to wink to them, the vibe check is very important - never, ever, forget that. 

A last small hint for you, unkindled one, if you never played this game and want to give it a try: 
USE WHAT YOU GET, the game is (most of the times lmao) not cruel to you, you are cruel to yourself. Because you can easily forget to use what you have and you "could" handle situations in a different way to progress deeper into the rabbit hole.

This rabbit hole changes your live. 


Micdrop.

Do not be scared of the dodge, rolls and parries.  There is still a community out there of people willing to help out.  I was helped plenty of times, and had the distinct pleasure of helping others in turn.

positive.original:
Some developer decisions degrade the gameplay experience. Some bosses, although large, are completely unreadable due to the camera angle. It's simply awful. The 21:9 monitor format isn't supported, causing black bars to appear on the sides. The game is designed to be played with a controller, and if you play with a mouse/keyboard, all in-game actions are mapped to the controller, such as pressing Y, R1, and so on. The quests are simply terrible. Without the wiki, they're impossible to complete. To get 100% of the achievements, you need to participate in PvP and defeat around 130 opponents, or farm just 2-3 mobs with a 1% item drop rate. Which is pure mockery.
Overall, the game is nice.

positive.original:
[h1]Dark Souls III Review[/h1]

[hr]
[h1]Overview[/h1]
Dark Souls III has been an absolute blast to play.

I decided to jump into it right after finishing Dark Souls 1 and 2, where I also went for all the achievements. I had tried Dark Souls III in the past for about 15 minutes and quit, but this time I knew I couldn’t skip it.

I had heard a lot of great things about this game, and honestly, I’m very glad I gave it a proper chance.

There are a lot of improvements here compared to the previous two games. While I wouldn’t say it completely replaces what made the first two special, Dark Souls III is easily the most polished and refined experience in the series.

[hr]
[h1]What It Is[/h1]
Dark Souls III takes place in the kingdom of Lothric, a world that is collapsing as the fire that sustains it begins to fade.

You play as the Ashen One, a being tasked with returning the Lords of Cinder to their thrones and deciding the fate of the world.

Just like the previous games, the story is not directly explained. You uncover it through exploration, item descriptions, NPC interactions, and environmental storytelling.

The game focuses on traveling through different areas, defeating powerful bosses, and slowly understanding the world and your role in it.

[hr]
[h1]Combat and Gameplay[/h1]
The combat in Dark Souls III is easily the best in the series.

It feels faster, smoother, and far more responsive than the previous games. Everything just feels more polished. After finishing Dark Souls 1 and 2, the difference was immediately noticeable.

Attacks, dodges, and overall movement feel much better, and the game is far more enjoyable to play because of it.

If the older games felt too slow or clunky, Dark Souls III completely fixes that.

The gameplay still keeps the classic Dark Souls formula, but it feels much more refined and modern, which made the experience much more enjoyable overall.

[hr]
[h1]Bosses[/h1]
The bosses in Dark Souls III are some of the best in the series.

They are large, intense, and very memorable. Each fight feels like a proper challenge, and learning their patterns was incredibly fun.

Because the combat is more polished, even dying repeatedly to bosses didn’t feel as frustrating. It always felt like I had the tools to improve and eventually win.

Some of these fights are easily among the most memorable in the entire series.

[hr]
[h1]World and Exploration[/h1]
Just like the previous games, Dark Souls III delivers a beautiful and dark world.

The atmosphere is still there. That same eerie feeling, that same sense of danger, and that same mysterious tone follow you throughout the entire game.

The world feels different from the previous games, yet still connected to the same universe. The architecture, enemies, and overall design make it feel familiar but fresh at the same time.

Exploration is still very enjoyable. There are secrets to find, different paths to take, and a good variety of environments and enemies.

However, the game is noticeably more linear than Dark Souls 1. The world feels more straightforward and less interconnected.

This wasn’t a big issue for me, but it is something worth mentioning.

[hr]
[h1]What Works[/h1]
[list]
[*]Best combat in the series, smooth and responsive
[*]Incredible and memorable boss fights
[*]Strong atmosphere and world design
[*]Polished gameplay compared to previous games
[*]Great enemy variety and fun exploration
[/list]

[hr]
[h1]What Falls Short[/h1]
[list]
[*]More linear world compared to Dark Souls 1
[*]Does not introduce many new mechanics
[*]Feels like a refined version rather than something new
[*]Reuses ideas and themes from previous games
[*]No ultrawide support without mods (forces offline play)
[/list]

[hr]
[h1]Verdict[/h1]
Dark Souls III is an incredible game and a fantastic conclusion to the series.

It may not introduce many new ideas, but it takes everything that worked in the previous games and refines it into a much smoother and more enjoyable experience.

If you are new to the series, this is probably one of the best starting points. If you already played the previous games, you will feel right at home.

Either way, it is absolutely worth playing.

positive.original: This game has undoubtedly change my life, I Know that's kinda cringe, but just hear me out okay. I had never played a fromsoft game before this one, I vividly remember  seeing the trailer for this game and thinking to myself. ♥♥♥♥ I love sword combat/medieval settings, unaware of the path I was going to set myself upon. Younger me was brash, hotheaded, and had zero patience. I had gotten stuck on the FIRST lothric knight, I could not beat him and unfortunately broke a controller in my anger, that's just who i was at that stage in my life. I had put the game down for such a long time but, it had always bothered me that i spent money on this game and never beat it, so I had picked the sticks back up to attempt the game that broke me. Going into the game with the mindset that I cannot quit, no obstacle will stop me from becoming what I had envisioned for myself, it was grueling honestly i got my ass kicked more often than not but i always went back and tried again. That's when I realized that these games aren't solely difficult fighting game that you need to learn combos for. These game represent so much more than that, it shows you the folly of man, but it also shows the determination of man. The only time you lose, truly, is when you close the game after a hard boss because you feel that the task is insurmountable. Understanding that one basic fact is enough to get you through anything difficult in you lives. All of the games that fromsoft puts out are littered with deeper messaging and lessons for you to learn. I love this game from the absolute bottom of my heart, my entire left arm is tattooed for this game. It fundamentally changed how I perceive difficult situations in my life and to never truly give into despair. Side note I had originally played this game on my xbox one when it came out I promise I'm not larping. Long may the sun shine upon all those who perceiver through whatever is getting you down.

Edit: the bosses do get better in the latter half of the game, the dlc's are also pretty kino. Get it on sale tho.

positive.original:
Dark Souls III stands as an extraordinary achievement in interactive art, a masterwork that exemplifies precision, atmosphere, and design philosophy at the highest level. It is not merely a game, but a meticulously crafted experience that rewards patience, curiosity, and mastery with a depth rarely matched in modern gaming.

From the very first moments, the world design commands admiration. The Cemetery of Ash introduces players with solemn elegance, its quiet desolation culminating in the unforgettable encounter with Iudex Gundyr, a brilliantly designed gatekeeper whose transformation sets the tone for the journey ahead. Firelink Shrine serves as a masterful hub—serene, melancholic, and steeped in mystery—anchoring the entire experience with understated grace.

The High Wall of Lothric rises as a triumph of introductory level design, its towering battlements and dragon-scorched ramparts guiding players through encounters with Vordt of the Boreal Valley, whose imposing presence and thunderous movements create an unforgettable early spectacle. The Undead Settlement follows with remarkable tonal contrast, its grim, lived-in horror populated by grotesque inhabitants and culminating in the Curse-Rotted Greatwood, a grotesque yet fascinating embodiment of decay.

The Road of Sacrifices and Crucifixion Woods offer a masterclass in atmosphere and tension, leading into the scholarly grandeur of the Cathedral of the Deep, where the Deacons of the Deep present a uniquely conceptual and visually striking battle. Farron Keep, with its oppressive swamp and haunting ruins, is elevated by the Abyss Watchers—one of the most iconic and elegant boss encounters ever crafted, a tragic dance of fire and steel.

The Catacombs of Carthus descend into skeletal chaos, culminating in the skeletal monarch High Lord Wolnir, whose scale and presentation evoke awe. Smouldering Lake expands this subterranean realm into a volcanic spectacle, where the Old Demon King stands as a poignant relic of a fading age.

Irithyll of the Boreal Valley is nothing short of breathtaking—an ethereal city bathed in moonlight, leading to the majestic confrontation with Pontiff Sulyvahn, whose relentless aggression and regal menace define excellence in boss design. The Church of Yorshka and Anor Londo further elevate the experience, the latter reintroduced with reverence and grandeur, culminating in Aldrich, Devourer of Gods, a haunting and deeply unsettling encounter.

Irithyll Dungeon and the Profaned Capital shift the tone into oppressive dread, their labyrinthine design leading to Yhorm the Giant, whose tragic narrative and cinematic presence elevate the encounter into something profoundly memorable.

Lothric Castle and the Grand Archives represent the pinnacle of architectural brilliance, their intricate layouts and verticality culminating in Dragonslayer Armour, a visually spectacular and mechanically refined battle. The ascent concludes with the Twin Princes, Lorian and Lothric, whose emotionally resonant and mechanically intricate fight stands among the finest in the medium.

The Consumed King’s Garden and Untended Graves provide haunting reflections of the world’s decay, featuring Oceiros, the Consumed King—eerily tragic in both design and lore—and Champion Gundyr, a triumphant reimagining of the game’s opening trial, now refined into pure mastery.

Archdragon Peak rises as a hidden marvel, its storm-lashed heights culminating in the Ancient Wyvern’s grand spectacle and the Nameless King, an encounter of unparalleled majesty and difficulty, widely regarded as one of the greatest boss fights ever created.

The Kiln of the First Flame serves as a perfect finale—ashen, silent, and timeless—where the Soul of Cinder embodies the legacy of all who came before. It is a poetic, mechanically brilliant conclusion that encapsulates the entire journey with profound elegance.

The combat system throughout is nothing short of exemplary. It achieves a flawless balance between responsiveness and weight, ensuring that every movement, strike, and dodge carries consequence. The diversity of weapons and builds allows for remarkable player expression while maintaining rigorous fairness. Every enemy, from the lowliest hollow to the most formidable knight, is placed with intention, contributing to a world that feels both dangerous and deliberate.

The atmosphere is unparalleled. A pervasive sense of melancholy and fading grandeur permeates every location, enhanced by exceptional art direction that balances beauty with decay. Lighting, scale, and environmental detail are executed with extraordinary precision, making every step through Lothric feel meaningful.

The musical score is profoundly evocative, elevating every major encounter. Boss themes swell with operatic intensity, transforming battles into unforgettable spectacles of emotion and tension. Each composition feels perfectly tailored, reinforcing the identity of every confrontation.

Narrative delivery remains subtle yet deeply impactful. Through item descriptions, environmental storytelling, and fragmented dialogue, the game constructs a rich tapestry of lore centered on cycles, sacrifice, and the inevitable passage of time. It respects the player’s intelligence, inviting interpretation rather than dictating meaning.

Technical execution and polish further solidify its excellence. Animations are fluid, controls are precise, and the presentation reflects an extraordinary level of craftsmanship. Every system feels deliberate, every detail considered.

In every conceivable aspect—world design, boss encounters, combat, atmosphere, music, and narrative—Dark Souls III achieves an extraordinary level of quality. Every area is memorable, every boss encounter a work of art, and every moment contributes to a cohesive and masterfully executed whole. A definitive 10/10, it stands as a landmark achievement in gaming—an experience of enduring brilliance and unparalleled refinement.

The diversity of weapons and builds allows for remarkable player expression while maintaining rigorous fairness. Every enemy, from the lowliest hollow to the most formidable knight, is placed with intention, contributing to a world that feels both dangerous and deliberate.

The atmosphere is unparalleled. A pervasive sense of melancholy and fading grandeur permeates every location, enhanced by exceptional art direction that balances beauty with decay. Lighting, scale, and environmental detail are executed with extraordinary precision, making every step through Lothric feel meaningful.

The musical score is profoundly evocative, elevating every major encounter. Boss themes swell with operatic intensity, transforming battles into unforgettable spectacles of emotion and tension. Each composition feels perfectly tailored, reinforcing the identity of every confrontation.

Through item descriptions, environmental storytelling, and fragmented dialogue, the game constructs a rich tapestry of lore centered on cycles, sacrifice, and the inevitable passage of time. It respects the player’s intelligence, inviting interpretation rather than dictating meaning.

Technical execution and polish further solidify its excellence. Animations are fluid, controls are precise, and the presentation reflects an extraordinary level of craftsmanship. Every system feels deliberate, every detail considered.

In every conceivable aspect—world design, boss encounters, combat, atmosphere, music, and narrative—Dark Souls III achieves an extraordinary level of quality. Every area is memorable, every boss encounter a work of art, and every moment contributes to a cohesive and masterfully executed whole. A definitive 10/10, it stands as a landmark achievement in gaming—an experience of enduring brilliance and unparalleled refinement.

positive.original:
The final entry of the original game that laid the foundation for the Souls-like genre. I completed it 100% on PS4 years ago, and this time I came back to do it again on Steam out of nostalgia -- and it’s still just as fun as ever.

It’s a bit unfortunate that the game isn’t well optimized for modern CPUs anymore. Even after fixing some issues myself, there are still occasional stutters. That said, it doesn’t significantly hurt the overall experience.

If you’re looking for a starting point for Souls-like games that’s more accessible than the first title, I highly recommend this one.

positive.original: Ds3 my goat. This was my first Dark Souls game so it will always hold a special place in my heart. However coming back from Eldenring the clunk and missing quality of life pretty apparent. When I first played the game I think the only area I had fps problems with was area before and during the Dragon Slayer armor. Was running on an Evga 750ti and a fx-6300 at 1080p. Have no problem with current hardware at 3440x1440. No ultrawide support or higher than 60 fps without mods ofc. I recommend it.

positive.original:
Great title that concluded the Souls trilogy and is probably the largest contributor to the Souls-like genre becoming mainstream. Replaying the game for the first time since launch i've come back with a newfound apprecaition of this title. Most importantly, the boss line up in DS3 is phenomenal and its base game and DLC easily have the strongest boss fights out of any souls title. Each boss is unique, there is a limited number of gimmick bosses and for a Souls-game there is a limited amount of bosses that create camera issues, thanks due to the fact Fromsoft didnt include many gigantic-mass type boss enemies. If you've played Elden Ring though I imagine the bosses will feel quite easy, given how slow they are in comparaison and the absence of delayed attakcs that were a common moveset for ER's bosses. At the time of release, DS3 was considered a leap from DS1/2's bosses in difficulty, these days its less pronouced as the community's skill-floor has developed with the genre. 

Game also runs at a rock-solid 60fps, not that you'd expect anything less given its age. But considering that Elden-Ring/Nightreign both suffer from shader-loading-related performance issues, its worth acknowledging that this isnt an issue in DS3. 

There is some more imperfect aspects: inconsistent hyper-armour from some enemies (not unique to DS3), Fromsoft's classic side-quest insanity which demands unnatural actions from players, to the covenant system being overally convoluted (there is too may, they are hard to naturally find and the rewards are a grind) in this game compared to other titles. The PvP is also simply less enjoyable and variable than DS2, in my opinon. I also wouldve liked some mix-up with the games colour palette, it pretty much retains the dark gothic colourway the entire playthrough and it becomes quite visually stale at times. I understand the thematic reasonings, but some contrasting areas/brightness wouldve been a nice visual cleanser that'd only further emphasised the truly bleak aspects of the game. 

None of this truly takes away from the expereince and DS3 remains a must-play for any Souls-like fan.

Most importantly, the boss line up in DS3 is phenomenal and its base game and DLC easily have the strongest boss fights out of any souls title. Each boss is unique, there is a limited number of gimmick bosses and for a Souls-game there is a limited amount of bosses that create camera issues, thanks due to the fact Fromsoft didnt include many gigantic-mass type boss enemies. If you've played Elden Ring though I imagine the bosses will feel quite easy, given how slow they are in comparaison and the absence of delayed attakcs that were a common moveset for ER's bosses. At the time of release, DS3 was considered a leap from DS1/2's bosses in difficulty, these days its less pronouced as the community's skill-floor has developed with the genre. 

Game also runs at a rock-solid 60fps, not that you'd expect anything less given its age. But considering that Elden-Ring/Nightreign both suffer from shader-loading-related performance issues, its worth acknowledging that this isnt an issue in DS3. 

There is some more imperfect aspects: inconsistent hyper-armour from some enemies (not unique to DS3), Fromsoft's classic side-quest insanity which demands unnatural actions from players, to the covenant system being overally convoluted (there is too may, they are hard to naturally find and the rewards are a grind) in this game compared to other titles. The PvP is also simply less enjoyable and variable than DS2, in my opinon. I also wouldve liked some mix-up with the games colour palette, it pretty much retains the dark gothic colourway the entire playthrough and it becomes quite visually stale at times. I understand the thematic reasonings, but some contrasting areas/brightness wouldve been a nice visual cleanser that'd only further emphasised the truly bleak aspects of the game. 

None of this truly takes away from the expereince and DS3 remains a must-play for any Souls-like fan.

positive.original:
After 2 whole playthroughs I thinks it's safe for me to say that I would recommend Dark Souls III to anyone who wants to try out the souls-like franchise. It's worth the price, especially if it's on sale.

Rating: 9/10

Pros:
-It has the best/most fluet combat of the entire Dark Souls franchise
-Amazing bosses especially in the late game
-Not to punishing for new players (spawnpoints, weapon durability, enemy placement, etc.)
-Fun weapons and build choses
-Visually stunning. The landscapes and views this game gives you are pretty damn breathtaking
-Memorable npc's and questlines

Cons:
-Level design is quiet linaire and just not engaging. 
  I only replay this game for new builds or to revisit the bosses that's it.
-The game can be incredible vague in directions and mechanics (no really try finding archdragon peak)
-IMO most areas aren't very memorable. A lot stone castle-like levels with repeated enemies.
-Mid game bosses kinda suck but they are ez anyway

Overall DS3 is one of my favourite games I've played in a long time. While it does lack a lot of personality other games have like DS1 it's still is an amazing game that serves as a good challenge while being a very breathtaking experience.

positive.original:
Orignally played it on PS4, before migrating to PC a few months ago. It was amazing on PS4. It's one of the best games I've ever played on PC.

Is it overpriced for how old it is? Well, yes. So pick it up on sale. Should happen during Summer and Winter sales.

But let it not be said that FromSoft wasn't cooking with this game. Massive recommend if you're looking to get into Soulsborne games, though admitably, the experience is elevated if you've played DS1 first.

Remember to download the Wex Dust mod, so it's easier to engage in PVP.

positive.original:
Cara, o que falar de Dark Souls 3? Bom, dando um contexto, esse jogo foi meu 2° Soulslike, sendo o primeiro Dark Souls 1, e aqui vemos uma melhora absurda em gameplay, graficos e bosses, mas nem tudo nesse jogo supera o 1°.

Vamos começar falando mais sobre os pontos positivos, Dark Souls 3 na minha concepção tem em maior vantagem a sua gameplay, ela é muito, e coloca muito nisso, mais fluida que a do primeiro jogo, aqui podemos ver que eles arriscaram muito mais ideias em bosses como a dançarina do vale boreal que é um dos bosses mais bem feitos da FromSoftware na minha opnião, temos lutas épicas contra chefes como Midir, Gael, Abbys watchers e etc... Claro que nem todas as ideias funcionam muito bem, como o Wolnir que se torna uma luta chata na verdade, pois tirando a névoa, ela é uma luta muito simples, mas que tinha mais potencial.

Agora vamos falar sobre alguns pontos negativos, se temos uma gameplay e bosses mais interessantes, aqui o nivel de level design na minha opinião peca bastante, em Dark Souls 1, nós tinhamos um mundo interconectado, parecendo até um metroidvania 3D, porém ele ta da a liberdade de explorar a vontade, e mesmo que ninguem te guie pro caminho certo, o jogo trabalha muito bem o nivel de dificuldade dos ambientes, coisa que não senti no 3, que além de ser linear, o nível de dificuldade desse jogo decai muito, o 3 é um jogo muito mais facil que o 1, e eu particularmente acho isso ruim, são poucos bosses no 3 que realmente dão trabalho, como o nameless king por exemplo

Mas tirando esses fatores ruins que novamente, são minha opinião e de forma alguma eu acredito que isso deixa o jogo ruim, esse jogo é uma obra de arte, tanto visualmente falando quanto sonora e narrativa, eu preciso parar pra escutar a musica do menu toda vez que eu entro no jogo.

Considerações finais, eu acho esse dark souls muito mais facil que os 2 anteriores, mas isso não tira sua beleza de maneira alguma, é um jogo lindo, divertido e com uma trilha sonora e narrativa impecavel, dito isso, nota: 9/10

positive.original:
First Dark Souls Game, plus Ashes of Ariandel and The Ringed City.
Wow.

Pros:
- Level and World Design. For a game that is not open world, there is so much to see and even more to find. From Software are the best at connecting levels and making exploration worthwhile. Curiosity is your best friend (though FromSoft always has something waiting for you around each corner). Favorite Locations: Irithyll of the Boreal Valley, The Ringed City, and Lothric Castle.
- Variety in enemies and bosses. I played as a sword and shield for most of the game. While your attacks can be limiting, the combat never got boring because there were always new enemies in new environments.
- Overall Lore and Narrative. I ended watching Vaatividya's videos on lore for DS1 and DS2, and whenever I beat a boss, I watched DS3 videos. I found myself reading all the item descriptions, but I never do so in other games. Though there are few cutscenes, there is so much depth in the lore.

Well done, Ashen One.

- Variety in enemies and bosses. I played as a sword and shield for most of the game. While your attacks can be limiting, the combat never got boring because there were always new enemies in new environments.
- Overall Lore and Narrative. I ended watching Vaatividya's videos on lore for DS1 and DS2, and whenever I beat a boss, I watched DS3 videos. I found myself reading all the item descriptions, but I never do so in other games. Though there are few cutscenes, there is so much depth in the lore.

Well done, Ashen One.

The Ringed City as a dlc definitely carried this game

positive.original:
[h1] DO NOT PLAY THE DLC BEFORE FINISHING THE MAIN GAME [/h1] 

Just a friendly advice to those people who have bought the DLC starting a new game and thinking if they should do the DLC first before finishing the final main boss of the game. This game does [b] NOT [/b] automatically bring you to NG+ and you will have an option after the end credit scene either [YES] or [NO] if you wanna continue. If you choose [NO] then you will just be brought back to the [b] Firelink Shrine [/b] and then you can do the DLC. And if you rest in the Bonfire, it will add an option whether you want to proceed with NG+ so you can start whenever you want. 

In my experience, finishing all the DLCs ruined the immersion for the final boss of this game due to bosses in the DLC tends to be more challenging [spoiler] IM TALKING ABOUT YOU SISTER FRIEDE [/spoiler] and making the final boss look ridiculously easy and underwhelming (at least from my experience). And yes, I might have been too overleveled after finishing the DLC but that's exactly why in my opinion, it's better to finish the main game first if you don't want to ruin the immersion for the ending of the game. 

But in all honesty, you can play the game however you want. Play the DLCs whenever you want, and experience it to yourself. You can enjoy the game however you want it to be, I'm just giving my opinion from my experience because I truly LOVE this game so much.

positive.original: Souls games require an entirely different approach than most games you could know. Every location, every corridor, every enemy is a challenge, and it's not about beating it, but about mastering it. Once you get the hang of it, the game is extremely rewarding. It's one of these somewhat rare occasions in gaming where you can feel that it's not your character that is leveling up and getting stronger. It's you as the player who improves the most as you play it, and it is a very satisfying feeling when you realize how much you've learned.

positive.original: Hey, do you like doing the same thing over and over again, carefully repeating the same path, until you perfect the set of actions that allow you to progress a small but tangible amount closer to your goal? If so you should probably talk to a therapist about getting diagnosed, but also you'll probably enjoy this game. It looks like an action game, and reflexes are a significant part of the game, but it's a lot more cerebral than most action games, much of the game is not just about chewing through enemies, but carefully picking which enemies to fight, on which ground, and watching them for tells to figure out when to strike and when to defend. It's a good game, a series that defined a genera and deservedly so. Only downside is the story, it's pure giberish without external sources to explain it, but it's also very pretty, in a disturbing and tragic kind of way, which was enough of a pull for me to keep trying to move forward.

Yes, indeed. It is called Lothric, where the transitory lands of the Lords of Cinder converge. In venturing north, the pilgrims discovered the truth of the old words: "The fire fades and the lords go without thrones." When the link of the fire is threatened, the bell tolls, unearthing the old Lords of Cinders from their graves. Aldrich, Saint of the Deep. Farron's Undead Legion, the Abyss Watchers. Nameless, accursed Undead, unfit even to be cinder.

And so it is, that ash seeketh embers.

positive.original:
Do you like dark fantasy?
Do you find beauty in a melancholic world with no sign of hope?
This game has it ALL

You will hear a lot of things about Dark Souls, in 85%, that it’s hard, but let me tell you something. 
Yes, it can be hard, especially if you’re new to the genre and you have absolutely no idea what to do, but don’t worry my friend. We’re all been there haven’t we?
This game will bring you experience for the rest of your life. You will learn patience, you will find motivation in you, when you fail countless of times, but you still go and try more and more. Locations are beautiful, enemies and bosses are also beautiful. Lot of interesting NPC’s with great stories. Countless of weapons, amors etc.
Dont be disappointed, if you die 1x, or 20x on the same boss. Go somewhere else, get better and then come back. If you put the controller down, you will miss a lot of great things. In this game, you must find beauty in the pain. No one is gonna hold your hand and tell you what to do, or where to go. When I played DS3 for the first time, I just went by myself and finished the game with no issue. If you’re scared of being lost, or have no clue where to go next, watch some YT videos. The connection with Ds1 will bring a tear to your eye. Especially if Ds 1 was the first game you played. I completed all achievements on Ds 1, Ds 2 and Ds 3. Best thing to do, if you wanna experience everything in Dark Souls games. 
For me, Ds 3 is the easiest one, so if you’re not experienced.. start here. Best combo is Ds 1 and then Ds 3, since Ds 2 is not that connected. I have reviews on all dark souls games, so check it out!

Don't get me wrong, Elden Ring was a masterpiece, but it lost a lot of what made Dark Souls great. Worth a replay, or if you have not experienced it and coming from Elden Ring, DS3 is where it started. Susend your desbelief on the graphics (it is now more than 10 years old, but has aged well enough to still play in 2026.

positive.original: i love this game its amazing one of my favourites but i genuinely almost gave it a negative review and refunded it due to FPS issues for some reason when my game was on fullscreen i was barely pushing 20 FPS my PC is extremely good so its not because of this and when i tried changing it in the settings it would crash my game i looked online and tried many fixes none worked anyway if anyone has the same issue the fix for this is to go to /Users/Name/AppData/Roaming/DS3/GraphicsConfig.xml open it with notepad and edit the config manually change FULLSCREEN to WINDOW and make it match your res this will fix it and your game will run like butter

negative.original: This used to be my all time favorite game. Why is this still 60 dollars? Why is every DLC 15-25 dollars? It's 10 years later and this game: 1) runs less efficiently 2) costs the same. Bandai's marketing team is more concerned with releasing game breaking updates for its predecessors (DS1 remake, DS2 Scholars edition, even yours truly) than actually providing any active support for it's prior titles. Elden Ring? Great! Dark Souls 3? Wonderful! DS2, DS1, Bloodborne. All really nice. My wallet compared to another live support dark fantasy hype beast that's going to get a brick update in 1-2 years? Not having it! I don't care if your foundation game is the Bible dude these DLCS + base price tags / release state are total folly. This game doesn't even launch for me anymore and I tried to fix it for like 5 hrs. Like how is that modernly acceptable. It used to run A+.

negative.original:
My friend and I had gotten into Dark Souls around the same time, difference being I was playing the entire trilogy in order while he was just going to play this one, the third installment. By the time I finished the first two games, he wasn't even halfway done with this game and ultimately just stopped playing. I sneered to myself, "Of course he's just going to stop playing this game halfway through, just like most games he plays." I opened Dark Souls III for the first time, eager to zip past him in progress. Then I was enlightened.

This ♥♥♥♥ is ARSE. A full decade of me constantly being shoved in a virtual vat of "Dark Souls is the good one, Dark Souls II is the ♥♥♥♥ one, but Dark Souls III is the best one." for this. This game has taught me a valuable lesson to never have your expectations raised, so you can never be disappointed. People really love their boss rushes huh.

A straight line vs. a spider web is what I would compare DS3 to the previous two. In DS3 you get a short-lived, 20-30 hour adventure (maybe it's for the best) where you literally just go straight. What made Dark Souls, Dark Souls was not the bossfights, but the "beautifully ugly" maze of a world that we were placed in the center of, our objective to trailblaze and figure out our way to outline the entirety of that maze. The magic of immersing in these "beautifully ugly" areas and  discovering how interconnected the world was to each other is in my opinion the core value of Dark Souls.

I used the descriptor "beautifully ugly" a few times to talk about DS1 and 2, but I think most areas in DS3 are just ugly. They're uninspiring, with nothing in between the bonfire and the boss of the area. Little to no reward for straying away from the main path (if there even is an option to) in a water-down, plain boring world. At least the ♥♥♥♥♥♥ areas in the previous games were iconic because they were REALLY good at being ♥♥♥♥♥♥, but this game pissed me off the most because everytime I died, I was reminded everytime I had to trudge through this bland ass area with nothing to look forward to in between. I just wanted out. I just wanted to escape the slog and just get it over with. There are a few exceptions, with Irithyll of the Boreal Valley being my personal standout, but even then, it's still at most a B-tier out of S for me. If you combined the quality and enjoyment of all the areas in DS3, it still wouldn't even touch the masterpiece that is Brume Tower from DS2. A couple of the areas are just one-dimensional versions of areas from DS1. I had hope when I first encountered these parts, but. shoulda known.

The bosses are good. Great even. Still not worth trading everything else Dark Souls was supposed to offer for them though. Especially since they still can't dream of touching Elden Ring, Sekiro, and maybe Lies of P (currently playing) bosses. I'm convinced people are just okay with the glaringly short playtime cause they get to fight more bosses. Bosses, bosses, bosses, it's like somehow everyone who hadn't experienced Dark Souls saw memes about dying to bosses online and just all collectively started on Dark Souls III, expected nothing but cool bosses and having never had their standards set for the more important aspects since they haven't experienced the wonderful world the previous two had to offer. The bosses in DS1 and 2 were actually quite terrible, with little standouts. But that didn't matter. It was completely reversed. I was looking forward to mapping my way through the world and dreading the abominations of bosses. It didn't matter since I value worldbuilding and how the game makes me feel through environmental storytelling much more than a bossfight I can get over with in just a few. It just makes the standouts in the game stand out even more, which might be worth it for me.

The main consensus is that the graphics are more polished and I wouldn't disagree. But I much prefer the more muddied textures of the first two. It makes it feel much more dark fantasy to me which somehow made me more immersed in the world. I know this is a weird complaint, but the textures in DS3 look like TOO polished to the point where it kind of looks worse. Almost glossy. I'm an avid screenshot taker and I have 100 more screenshots on DS1 than DS3, even when the ladder has a lot more cinematic moments.

A chore. I felt the same playing this like I feel doing calculus homework.

A straight line vs. a spider web is what I would compare DS3 to the previous two. In DS3 you get a short-lived, 20-30 hour adventure (maybe it's for the best) where you literally just go straight. What made Dark Souls, Dark Souls was not the bossfights, but the "beautifully ugly" maze of a world that we were placed in the center of, our objective to trailblaze and figure out our way to outline the entirety of that maze. The magic of immersing in these "beautifully ugly" areas and  discovering how interconnected the world was to each other is in my opinion the core value of Dark Souls.

I used the descriptor "beautifully ugly" a few times to talk about DS1 and 2, but I think most areas in DS3 are just ugly. They're uninspiring, with nothing in between the bonfire and the boss of the area. Little to no reward for straying away from the main path (if there even is an option to) in a water-down, plain boring world. At least the ♥♥♥♥♥♥ areas in the previous games were iconic because they were REALLY good at being ♥♥♥♥♥♥, but this game pissed me off the most because everytime I died, I was reminded everytime I had to trudge through this bland ass area with nothing to look forward to in between. I just wanted out. I just wanted to escape the slog and just get it over with. There are a few exceptions, with Irithyll of the Boreal Valley being my personal standout, but even then, it's still at most a B-tier out of S for me. If you combined the quality and enjoyment of all the areas in DS3, it still wouldn't even touch the masterpiece that is Brume Tower from DS2. A couple of the areas are just one-dimensional versions of areas from DS1. I had hope when I first encountered these parts, but. shoulda known.

The bosses are good. Great even. Still not worth trading everything else Dark Souls was supposed to offer for them though. Especially since they still can't dream of touching Elden Ring, Sekiro, and maybe Lies of P (currently playing) bosses. I'm convinced people are just okay with the glaringly short playtime cause they get to fight more bosses. Bosses, bosses, bosses, it's like somehow everyone who hadn't experienced Dark Souls saw memes about dying to bosses online and just all collectively started on Dark Souls III, expected nothing but cool bosses and having never had their standards set for the more important aspects since they haven't experienced the wonderful world the previous two had to offer. The bosses in DS1 and 2 were actually quite terrible, with little standouts. But that didn't matter. It was completely reversed. I was looking forward to mapping my way through the world and dreading the abominations of bosses. It didn't matter since I value worldbuilding and how the game makes me feel through environmental storytelling much more than a bossfight I can get over with in just a few. It just makes the standouts in the game stand out even more, which might be worth it for me.

The main consensus is that the graphics are more polished and I wouldn't disagree. But I much prefer the more muddied textures of the first two. It makes it feel much more dark fantasy to me which somehow made me more immersed in the world. I know this is a weird complaint, but the textures in DS3 look like TOO polished to the point where it kind of looks worse. Almost glossy. I'm an avid screenshot taker and I have 100 more screenshots on DS1 than DS3, even when the ladder has a lot more cinematic moments.

A chore. I felt the same playing this like I feel doing calculus homework.

negative.original:
This game is unplayable on modern hardware. Constantly freezing for several seconds.
EDIT: the solution was to go into task manager > details > right click DS3 > set affinity > disable core 0.
It also sucks that there is no Steam cloud syncing so I have to copy over my save file from Appdata > roaming anytime I want to play on my other computer.
EDIT 2: ♥♥♥♥ this laggy game. Won't buy the DLC nor any of the other Dark Souls games.

It also sucks that there is no Steam cloud syncing so I have to copy over my save file from Appdata > roaming anytime I want to play on my other computer.
EDIT 2: ♥♥♥♥ this laggy game. Won't buy the DLC nor any of the other Dark Souls games.

negative.original:
I think playing this game is a bit of a chore. The world doesn't suck me in at all and the combat is clunky. "Get good" is the refrain, but I don't feel any desire to get good, really. When I quit this game it isn't because I'm ragequitting, it's because I'm bored and would rather just be doing something else. 
So therefore, I can't personally recommend this game. But clearly people love it, clearly it must be a good game. I just can't personally recommend it.

negative.original:
Worst of the trilogy, by far. 
The game brutally teaches you that the way to play, is to roll spam and then spam R1. 
Fast weapons are king, even light daggers stun enemies - while with anything slower, like a spear, you get punished. 
Blocking with a shield drains too much stamina to be viable. The only comfortable way to do so, is to have a 70+ stability greatshield with magic shield spell on it. 
Overall a huge huge huge letdown, and spits in the face of variety the previous two games had.

negative.original:
There's a lot of really great stuff here, A lot of terrible design decisions. The worst components of fromsoft design are cranked up to 11. Enemy spam. Duo Fights. Time wasting first phases. Obtuse questlines. Clunky controls. The camera still sucks. I really don't like how many traps there are.  A few is cute and funny, but when theres too many it feels like my time is being wasted. When every other chest is a mimic it's just another enemy instead of a funny little surprise.

negative.original:
Easily the worst game From Software has released since their rise to popularity due to Demon's Souls.  Total fanservice wankjob "lore" that feels like it was written so some goober Youtuber nerds can make crappy self-fellating videos and overall it feels like even the devs were bored of this series and wanted to move on.  And it shows since the games preceding and following Dark Souls 3, Bloodborne and Sekiro, are both VASTLY superior in every single way.  Dark Souls II had a ton of cool uniques and mechanics and they carried none of them over to DS3.  Play it if you finally discovered From Software because of Elden Ring and judge for yourself.  The first DLC release was awful as well.  

This game gets a free pass from a ton of criticism because fans were all, "Miyazaki senpai!!!!" was the lead and not the "B team" from Dark Souls 2.  Funny how a lot of the B team made Elden Ring as well.  Gamers are such hypocritical manbabies.

negative.original: like to endlessly dodge and never get a window? what about terrible crowd control fights where everything moves and attacks 1.5x faster than you? are you too tired of playing games that are actually fun and well designed? Ds3 is just for you! please dont waste your money this game is horrible. play ds1 and ds2, elden ring is faster but somehow way better than this. I regret the money I spent on this game and wish I never bought it. For the record I have about 200 hours in ds1 and probably over 1000 in ds2 im not new to fromsoftware but wow man this is terrible. have resorted to dupe glitches and thats just not very fun and its still just annoying. regular combat is not even fun or satisfying even when things are going well and im wrecking shop its just not very fun at all. feels like nothing has any weight to it. dodging is a big gripe I have I want to dodge an attack and come back with my own not just dodge endlessly to get through a combo that ends with the enemy far enough out of my attack range that  in closing the gap their entire recovery animation is over and its back to dodging. stun-lock or nothing I guess is what the devs said for this one and it really shows. some fights were good. tutorial boss, fun, challenging, thought provoking, scary when second phase starts, the boreal big dude idk his name hes forgettable but a fun fight, this one guy right before you get to the road of sacrifices. - he only took me three tries i thought okay im getting the hang of this- no it was just a rare sighting of a well designed enemy that wont be a common occurrence. other than that I have hated every enemy so far. souls is another thing its like they were scared that if they made enemies give you a good amount of souls itd make the game actually enjoyable so everything gives you next to no souls at all I dont even wanna think about trying to farm to level up that would take hours and I probably just lose it all anyways. theres more but thats all im going to say please please if youre new stay far away from this game and play ds2 I know i know the reputation it has but its so good and most of the issues people have with it are blown way out of proportion. after that delve into ds1 and enjoy it for the masterpeice that it is. ds3 gets 0/10 stars as a souls game 4/10 as a game. oh yeah and I hope your 100% color blind, you wont miss anything here because the whole game is in grayscale.

For the record I have about 200 hours in ds1 and probably over 1000 in ds2 im not new to fromsoftware but wow man this is terrible. have resorted to dupe glitches and thats just not very fun and its still just annoying. regular combat is not even fun or satisfying even when things are going well and im wrecking shop its just not very fun at all. feels like nothing has any weight to it. dodging is a big gripe I have I want to dodge an attack and come back with my own not just dodge endlessly to get through a combo that ends with the enemy far enough out of my attack range that  in closing the gap their entire recovery animation is over and its back to dodging. stun-lock or nothing I guess is what the devs said for this one and it really shows. some fights were good. tutorial boss, fun, challenging, thought provoking, scary when second phase starts, the boreal big dude idk his name hes forgettable but a fun fight, this one guy right before you get to the road of sacrifices. - he only took me three tries i thought okay im getting the hang of this- no it was just a rare sighting of a well designed enemy that wont be a common occurrence. other than that I have hated every enemy so far. souls is another thing its like they were scared that if they made enemies give you a good amount of souls itd make the game actually enjoyable so everything gives you next to no souls at all I dont even wanna think about trying to farm to level up that would take hours and I probably just lose it all anyways. theres more but thats all im going to say please please if youre new stay far away from this game and play ds2 I know i know the reputation it has but its so good and most of the issues people have with it are blown way out of proportion. after that delve into ds1 and enjoy it for the masterpeice that it is. ds3 gets 0/10 stars as a souls game 4/10 as a game. oh yeah and I hope your 100% color blind, you wont miss anything here because the whole game is in grayscale.

For the record I have about 200 hours in ds1 and probably over 1000 in ds2 im not new to fromsoftware but wow man this is terrible. have resorted to dupe glitches and thats just not very fun and its still just annoying. regular combat is not even fun or satisfying even when things are going well and im wrecking shop its just not very fun at all. feels like nothing has any weight to it. dodging is a big gripe I have I want to dodge an attack and come back with my own not just dodge endlessly to get through a combo that ends with the enemy far enough out of my attack range that  in closing the gap their entire recovery animation is over and its back to dodging. stun-lock or nothing I guess is what the devs said for this one and it really shows. some fights were good. tutorial boss, fun, challenging, thought provoking, scary when second phase starts, the boreal big dude idk his name hes forgettable but a fun fight, this one guy right before you get to the road of sacrifices. - he only took me three tries i thought okay im getting the hang of this- no it was just a rare sighting of a well designed enemy that wont be a common occurrence. other than that I have hated every enemy so far. souls is another thing its like they were scared that if they made enemies give you a good amount of souls itd make the game actually enjoyable so everything gives you next to no souls at all I dont even wanna think about trying to farm to level up that would take hours and I probably just lose it all anyways. theres more but thats all im going to say please please if youre new stay far away from this game and play ds2 I know i know the reputation it has but its so good and most of the issues people have with it are blown way out of proportion. after that delve into ds1 and enjoy it for the masterpeice that it is. ds3 gets 0/10 stars as a souls game 4/10 as a game. oh yeah and I hope your 100% color blind, you wont miss anything here because the whole game is in grayscale.

negative.original:
Dark Souls III is where things start to unravel. 
Not all at once, not in a dramatic collapse, but in a very clear shift in priorities.

Speed. Spectacle. Noise.

That’s the identity. That’s the pitch. That’s the problem.

I played it at launch, dropped it after about 15 hours thinking it just needed more time, like it wasn’t fully cooked yet. Came back years later, after patches and DLCs, expecting it to finally come together.

It didn’t. It’s still raw.

This is the most linear game in the Souls series. Not just in level layout, but in how the entire experience is structured. You move forward because the game pushes you forward. Exploration exists, but it’s secondary. The focus is on pacing and that pacing is built entirely around speed.

Or at least, the idea of speed.

Because what the game presents as fast, aggressive, high-intensity combat isn’t actually clean or precise. It’s noise. Mechanically, visually, and mentally. Everything is turned up animations, enemy aggression, effects but without the clarity or system depth to support it. So instead of feeling faster, it just feels cluttered.

Combat hasn’t evolved it’s been pushed. Underneath, it’s still the same formula. But now everything happens quicker, chains harder, hits louder. The problem is that the systems weren’t rebuilt for that tempo. So what you get is desync between what you see, what you do, and what actually happens.
Inputs feel slightly off. Enemy behavior feels inconsistent. Fights become less about deliberate action and more about reacting to a flood of movement and effects.

It’s not speed in the sense of mastery. It’s speed in the sense of saturation.

And the visuals double down on it.

Fog, haze, sparks, fire, bloom everything is layered on top of everything else. Not subtly, not to enhance, but to overwhelm. It often feels like these effects are doing more than setting the tone they’re covering for things. Hiding animation roughness, masking transitions, filling space.

But it doesn’t stop there. The game can’t decide how much detail it actually wants. One moment you’re staring at a screen so cluttered you can barely parse what’s happening. The next, you’re looking at something oddly flat, almost underbuilt. Then it swings the other way hyper-detailed armor, exaggerated faces, overdesigned enemies that look like they wandered in from a different game entirely.
There’s no middle ground. No consistency. Just constant shifting between too much and not enough.

From “what the hell am I even looking at”
to “this face has fewer polygons than a Morrowind NPC”
to “anime boss explosion, full effects, no survivors.”
And that constant swing reinforces the fatigue.

Not motion sickness, motion fatigue. Your eyes get tired. Your brain gets tired. Not because the game is demanding, but because it never settles. It never gives you a stable image to read or trust.
This is not atmosphere. It’s just noise.

Then there’s the camera. Still bad. Arguably worse here because of everything else going on. It gets caught in walls, lost in crowds, thrown around by elevation and movement. Combined with the visual clutter and forced tempo, it stops being a tool and starts being part of the problem.

You’re not just fighting enemies you’re fighting visibility. The camera. The speed. The noise.
How do you win against something that doesn’t even have an HP bar?

What makes this worse is that the old issues are still here. Enemy AI bugs out. Animations desync. That familiar FromSoftware “loop” still shows up where enemies or bosses freeze, stall, or just stop behaving. In slower games like Dark Souls or Dark Souls II, you could work around it. Here, you can’t. The speed exposes everything.

That’s the core failure. FromSoftware didn’t rebuild the system they accelerated it. But instead of achieving precision, they created friction. Instead of flow, they created noise.

Speed without clarity.
Spectacle without substance.
Noise without purpose.

There are good moments. Some bosses hit the mark. A few areas briefly capture that older Souls vibe, feeling structured, readable, deliberate. In those moments, the game almost works.

Verdict:
Not terrible. Not even bad. But fundamentally misguided.
It trades clarity for speed, depth for spectacle and ends up drowning in its own noise.

Not motion sickness, motion fatigue. Your eyes get tired. Your brain gets tired. Not because the game is demanding, but because it never settles. It never gives you a stable image to read or trust.
This is not atmosphere. It’s just noise.

How do you win against something that doesn’t even have an HP bar?

Not terrible. Not even bad. But fundamentally misguided.

negative.original:
Bonfire ascetics are gone,
Poise is gone,
Cannot fast climb ladders,
Lack of spell variety and items with special effects,
Dual wielding gone,
Spices are gone,
Environmental traps/utilities that you could turn to your advantage are gone,
Quests are designed to fail without prior esoteric knowledge;
extremely easy to lock yourself out of something if you don't follow a guide as you play,
PVP meta is panic rolling, use a light weapon and pray your connection is stronger than the opponents,
Can't place unwanted consumables in the storage,
Have to wait a full 5 seconds after each kill to see if there is a drop, and drops are attached to ragdoll bodies that easily fly off edges,
No cloudsaving so backup your files (but be aware that this is reported to have gotten players banned),
Decent game but definitely a regression in design.

negative.original:
I've been playing Dark Souls since 2017. I love the games, they mean a lot to me and I cherish them, even though they all are flawed. But Dark Souls III is... a mixed bag for me.

I enjoy the game. I love the PvP, I've spent just as much time on learning it's PvP as I have Dark Souls II's. It's fun, it's surprisingly still active if you know where to look, and it's in-depth and cool to learn.

My main (and only) issue is how much of it is just... stuff ripped from Dark Souls I and II. How your character feels to play, a lot of the movesets, models, etc, are just ripped from the older games and it really shows. It doesn't feel unique at all. I do understand why from a lore perspective, but even then it just didn't feel artistically creative. While it is cool to reference the older games, having nearly the whole game be references to older stuff makes it feel lazy and uncreative, drags down a lot of the artistic integrity the game has. I do enjoy the game more than Dark Souls I, mostly because it plays like a more refined version of the first game's combat, but I always have the one voice in the back of my mind telling me that it's just Dark Souls I.
A lot of the game isn't unique. That's the main issue I have with it. I'd love to rate it higher, but I honestly just can't. If they did more unique things like DS2 did, I'd vastly reconsider it. But as it is, it's an 8/10 at the highest. The DLCs add a good 2-3 points.

negative.original:
[h1]The third and final installment of the ground-breaking and genre defining Dark Souls series: to me a crushing disappointment.[/h1]

I'll start by briefly defining what made Dark Souls as great as it was....

In 2009, Demon's Souls, Dark Souls' predecessor, was released and adored in the West, but not so much in the East. This reaction led to the creation, but most importantly the release of Dark Souls in 2011. This game would go on to receive the "Greatest game of all time" award, cementing itself as a pillar of "modern" gaming. Seeing the immense success of the game, a sequel was ordered. However, the director had decided to work on another game. The task to direct Dark Souls 2 was given to one, passed to another and finally was finished and released in 2014. Yet again, the public loved it and complimented the greatness of the game. Nearly perfect scores by some critics, though the fanbase itself would end up being very divided on the game. Then, the year 2015 came along, with a re-release of Dark Souls 2. Only one year later, Dark Souls 3 came out. 

I had played Dark Souls 1 for nearly 1300 hours, and Dark Souls 2 for ~800 at the time of my first experience with Dark Souls 3. I LOVED both prequels to an unimaginable extent. It was nearly an obsession. I thought that, if the 2 others were this grand, and that, in my opinion, Dark Souls 2 was a major improvement on Dark Souls 1, surely Dark Souls 3 would be the greatest game of all time! I was severely mistaken, though...

Dark Souls (the series) relied on slow-pace combat and encouraged the player to pay attention to small details and worry about positioning. The combat was simple: Light and heavy attacks, directional dodges based on camera lock, two hands for one weapon/tool each. Simple as that. It worked so well and Dark Souls 2 kept it, adding more options for using both hands for weapons, as well. The combat was a test of patience and adaptability (not the attribute in DS2) more so than skill. The games were grounded, slow and clunky, but felt good to play. Then, Dark Souls 3 came out. Following the success of Bloodborne, released in 2014, worked on at the same time as Dark Souls 2, Dark Souls 3 would reimagine the combat, a signature element of the series so far. The game became less focused on adventure, with a linear map. Less focused on characters, by using simple archetypes or returning faces. Less focused on being creative and different, reusing animations, designs and move sets from previous games. It instead focused on the bosses. While the combat in Dark souls was always central, it wasn't the biggest or main selling point. Players, however, loved the bosses the most, as they stood as tests for the player to see how far they've come. However, the games also had expansive worlds and so many options handed to the player, whether it be the path you take or the quests you do. Dark Souls 3 forces you down a straight line, with very few optional areas. The few that are there are hidden, as well, making it seem like the game is one long road with a few bosses. Despite the game shifting focus on the bosses, changing the core feeling of the combat to something quicker and more floaty, in my opinion, it failed dramatically at making quality bosses. The 2 others had walked away from the pure gimmick fights of Demon's Souls, focusing on action combat instead, but still kept it slow and gimmicky at times. Dark Souls 3 fails its gimmick fights horribly, though. The game would excel at making fast-paced battles work with its movement, but the low amount of total bosses means a high percentage of them are failed gimmick fights, which are sad callbacks to when they could work in the others. Even then, the fights it took from were already laughably easy or bad in the other games, so it dug its grave deeper by not adapting to its own changes. It tried to stray from the old school Dark Souls, but its roots were firmly planted in the path it dearly wished not to follow. The action packed fights also tend to fail, in my opinion, by their design. The other games had a lot of room for adaptation. Dark Souls 3 wants you to play a certain way, and not doing so will make it much worse to play through the game.

The game also suffers from bugs. So many bugs. The most glaring and apparent issue is the shader problem. It's commonly joked about that the game looks grey. Well, yeah, it does. Because the game has a massive problem with its shaders. There's some grey filter over the whole game. Colors stand out more when they're allowed through, but overall, every area has one dominant color, which works artistically and story-wise, but gets exceedingly boring when you walk out of a grey castle to enter a grey village, to reach a grey church through a brown and grey swamp. This isn't hyperbolic, I described the path from the High Wall to the Cathedral, while being kind enough to leave the Cemetery and Shrine out of it. Outside of that, it suffers a lot from its quicker gameplay being affected by framerate. This can cause attacks to flail and their hitboxes to break. The camera was always awkward, but this game pushes it up to 11. Entities that chase you and are outside of your PoV will teleport behind you at times, especially noticeable on dogs. The Nameless King has an attack that can be completely ignored if you pan your camera away and leave him out of frame. This does NOT happen in the other games. It also has horrible collision problems. The ground sometimes stops working, and you either float or fall through, running attacks with greatswords on illusory walls can send you through the floor, I've clipped through walls and floor with ladders, and the Lothric Castle area has walls without collisions that have crossbow-wielding soldiers behind it, who can spot and shoot you through said walls. While minor, these issues pile up and can drastically affect the player's experience. All the issues I described happened to me, and those are all from my first playthrough. Some happened on other characters too. The game also has a problem with textures and when to load them. Going down the huge ladder in the Profaned Capital, if you look down, the floor's textures take a while to load sometimes, letting you see a mushy and ugly textures mess. The same happens with the wall near the Mercenary's Armor set in the Crucifixion Woods. There are many areas that let you see from up close the out-of-bounds sections, which are very poorly textured and low quality. This is excusable, but they could have tried to keep it out of clear and plain sight. The other games, while older, manage to mostly avoid the issue, or cover it up with some scenery. 

I wanted to love this game. I tried. For around 250 hours I tried and couldn't. This will forever be my least favorite game of the series. Dark Souls 2 is often called the black sheep, but Dark Souls 3 is far more deserving of the title, for being so blindingly different to its predecessors. It lost the core formulas and wasted most chances it got. The DLCs are fine, but do not excuse or redeem the mess that the base game is, because the central issues remain present. I will forever be disappointed that this is what we were given as a close to my favorite game series of all time. As unpopular as my opinion is, I feel shame saying I love the series, only because this game is part of it. 

If you like it, that's fine. I won't judge or hate you for it. However, some of its issues cannot be ignored and as much as I wish I could look past them, it's impossible for me to recommend the game, even to fans of the genre that came from the other FromSoftware titles. This game isn't a complete disgrace, but it has tarnished my opinion of the series as a whole severely enough to not be forgiven.

Then, the year 2015 came along, with a re-release of Dark Souls 2. Only one year later, Dark Souls 3 came out. 

I had played Dark Souls 1 for nearly 1300 hours, and Dark Souls 2 for ~800 at the time of my first experience with Dark Souls 3. I LOVED both prequels to an unimaginable extent. It was nearly an obsession. I thought that, if the 2 others were this grand, and that, in my opinion, Dark Souls 2 was a major improvement on Dark Souls 1, surely Dark Souls 3 would be the greatest game of all time! I was severely mistaken, though...

The combat was simple: Light and heavy attacks, directional dodges based on camera lock, two hands for one weapon/tool each. Simple as that. The combat was a test of patience and adaptability (not the attribute in DS2) more so than skill. The games were grounded, slow and clunky, but felt good to play. Then, Dark Souls 3 came out. Dark Souls 2 is often called the black sheep, but Dark Souls 3 is far more deserving of the title, for being so blindingly different to its predecessors.
